source.title: The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits
source.authors: Shuming Ma; Hongyu Wang; Lingxiao Ma; Lei Wang; Wenhui Wang; Shaohan Huang; Li Dong; Ruiping Wang; Jilong Xue; Furu Wei

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures validation perplexity and downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, but uses a different model and training setup from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation perplexity by model size and downstream accuracy by model size. It does not fit power laws or report predictions from smaller runs. Latency, memory, throughput and energy results are not rows because they do not measure the claim's loss or downstream-performance outcomes. The 2T-token comparison in Table 4 is not a test of predictable change with tokens.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It compares ternary-weight BitNet b1.58 with reproduced FP16 LLaMA at three to four sizes (700M–3.9B, under one order of magnitude), all at 100B tokens. It fits no power law, makes no extrapolation, does no compute-allocation sweep, and fits no downstream prediction. Its 'new scaling law' is a cost-equivalence statement (e.g. 13B BitNet cheaper than 3B FP16), not a loss power law. Perplexity and accuracy falling or rising with size are incidental to the method comparison. They cannot establish power-law form or predictability.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say BitNet b1.58 matches FP16 LLaMA in perplexity and zero-shot accuracy from 3B at equal size and tokens, while costing far less in latency, memory, throughput and energy. Their 'new scaling law' refers to performance-versus-inference-cost equivalences (e.g. 13B BitNet cheaper than 3B FP16), not a fitted loss power law.
record.recipe_differences: BitNet b1.58 is trained from scratch with ternary weights and 8-bit activations; the paper compares it with reproduced FP16 LLaMA models rather than fitting the original scaling-law recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Model family and parameter count vary. The paper does not report sensitivity to loss-fitting method or other scaling-law fit choices.

fits_no_version.finding: The ternary-weight model trails FP16 at 700M (PPL 12.87 vs 12.33) but matches or beats it at 3B (9.91 vs 10.04). The authors say the gap narrows with size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The loss gap between low-precision (ternary) and full-precision LMs trained from scratch shrinks with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: The 'new scaling law' is an inference-cost equivalence: 13B/30B/70B BitNet is cheaper than 3B/7B/13B FP16. It is derived from latency, memory and energy measurements, not loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-bit models shift the performance-versus-inference-cost frontier.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the perplexity or task scores. The perplexity table does not identify which validation dataset each value corresponds to. The paper reports no power-law fit, extrapolation test or compute-optimal allocation test.
record.rows_left_out: Three Table 2 task-score rows are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit: LLaMA LLM ARC-Easy at 700M, 1.3B and 3B. These task scores are 54.7, 56.9 and 62.1. Table 4's 2T-token comparison and cost-only measurements are also not included because they do not test the extracted scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Power-law form, several orders of magnitude, and token or compute scaling are all untested. There are only 3–4 sizes at fixed 100B tokens.
All of V2: no extrapolation from small runs.
All of V3: no compute-optimal allocation.
All of V4: no shape sweep.
No predictive fit from scale or loss to downstream scores.
All of V7: no exponent fits or fit-choice comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: I reclassify this from tests/T2 to discusses/T6: the size sweep is under one decade, with no fits, at a single token count. The reader's V1 and V6 labels are removed. Per-task L and B rows are unlinked because the averages (D rows) already cover them and no row can show predictability. Table 1 gives one PPL column although the text names both WikiText2 and C4.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports perplexity across parameter counts, but does not fit or establish a power-law form, test several orders of magnitude, or vary tokens or compute.
No smaller-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is reported.
The paper does not compare depth, width or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
The paper studies text pretraining from scratch, not other modalities, repeated-data scaling, fine-tuning or transfer scaling.
The paper reports downstream scores at several sizes, but does not fit a predictive relationship or test prediction from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents or curve shapes is reported.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: LLaMA LLM and BitNet b1.58 at 700M–3.9B, trained on 100 billion tokens
reader_labels.reason: Perplexity decreases across the reported sizes, but the tested range is limited and the paper does not fit a power law; see P1–P7.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported seven-task average scores at the tested sizes
reader_labels.reason: The reported average rises with size for both model families; see D1–D7.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Individual task scores across the tested sizes
reader_labels.reason: Some scores are not monotonic, including BitNet BoolQ and OpenbookQA and LLaMA BoolQ and Winogrande; the tables also do not fit or validate predictions. See B13–B20, L7–L18.
